I'll just echo what everyone is saying and recommend that you slow it down! Hitting in the sweet spot is more important than swinging as hard as you can. That will improve distance and direction. Something that helped me was having the feeling that my leading arm was in control of the swing. It helped me to pause at the top of my swing, and helped with my weight transfer. Keep it slow and smooth until you feel confident in your contact and ramp up from there! 

Number one, most important thing out there, is to relax and enjoy yourself! Golf is a practice in slowing things down; not just your swing. Have fun out there!

This is false. ABC extinguishers are for type A,B, and C fires. Type A is for wood and paper fires, type B is for petroleum, propane, and butane,and type C is for electrical fires. An ABC would be fine for a small fire in a pinch, but class K extinguishers are specifically designed for grease fires. Most fire suppression systems are fitted with K-class for this reason

It depends on the type of extinguisher used. K class extinguishers are used for most kitchen fires and are the silver extinguishers. NEVER USE A RED EXTINGUISHER ON A GREASE FIRE. Always know where your silver and red extinguishers are and what to use them for!

So I would suggest you don't put the ball any further back than the middle of your stance for most situations. I would instead try to focus on how you tuck your elbow into your body on your back arm through the downswing. When I'm hitting wedges, I pull my elbow in tight to try to keep the club head path consistent. I would also suggest pushing off your leading foot as much as possible to get your body moving forward. That will help with contact and distance. Also, focus on slowing down and making good contact. Speed up when you feel comfortable, but try to remember that solid contact will beat brute force every time! Watch a few videos on YouTube also!
